```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "htbp", out.extra = ""
)

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
  library(kableExtra)
  library(patchwork)
})

source(file.path("..", "R", "03-fit-models.R"))

processed <- readRDS(file.path("..", "data", "processed", "marathon.rds"))
all_finishers <- processed$all_finishers
run <- processed$analysis

fits <- fit_marathon_models(run)
primary <- fits$primary
log_model <- fits$log_log

coefs <- coef(primary)
b0 <- coefs[["(Intercept)"]]
b1 <- coefs[["half_min"]]
fit_summary <- summary(primary)
diag <- model_diagnostics(primary)

slope_classical <- test_slope(primary, benchmark = 2)
slope_robust <- test_slope(primary, benchmark = 2, robust = TRUE)
log_slope <- test_slope(log_model, benchmark = 1)

n_analysis <- nrow(run)
n_finishers <- nrow(all_finishers)
n_dropped <- n_finishers - n_analysis

pct_positive <- 100 * mean(run$second_half_min > run$half_min)
median_ratio <- median(run$split_ratio)

# Minutes by which the doubling rule falls short of the fitted prediction at a
# given halfway split: (beta0 + beta1 * x) - 2x.
shortfall <- function(x) b0 + (b1 - 2) * x
median_split <- median(run$half_min)
shortfall_median <- shortfall(median_split)
split_at_15min <- (15 - b0) / (b1 - 2)
pct_over_15min <- 100 * mean(run$half_min > split_at_15min)
# Halfway split at which the fitted line crosses the even-pacing line y = 2x.
split_crossing <- -b0 / (b1 - 2)
n_below_crossing <- sum(run$half_min < split_crossing)

spread_raw <- residual_spread_by_bin(primary, run$half_min)
spread_log <- residual_spread_by_bin(log_model, log(run$half_min))
spread_ratio_raw <- max(spread_raw$resid_sd) / min(spread_raw$resid_sd)
spread_ratio_log <- max(spread_log$resid_sd) / min(spread_log$resid_sd)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 10))
theme_update(
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")
)

fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
hms <- function(minutes) {
  total <- round(minutes * 60)
  sprintf("%d:%02d:%02d", total %/% 3600, (total %% 3600) %/% 60, total %% 60)
}
```


The code used to download, prepare, and analyze the data is available at
<https://github.com/pujithabobbili/simple-regression-project>.

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Doubling a runner's halfway time is an easy way to estimate a marathon
finishing time. It assumes that the runner will take the same amount of time
for both halves. I examined how well this rule worked for the 2023 Boston
Marathon, using official results available through the SCORE Network Sports
Data Repository [@fay2023boston]. After excluding finishers without a halfway
split, the analysis included `r fmt(n_analysis, 0)` runners. I fitted a simple
linear regression with net finishing time as the response and half-marathon
split as the predictor, both measured in minutes. The estimated slope was
`r fmt(b1, 3)`, with a conventional 95% confidence interval of
`r fmt(slope_classical$conf_low, 3)` to `r fmt(slope_classical$conf_high, 3)`.
This is above the slope of 2 implied by equal times for the two halves. About
`r fmt(pct_positive, 0)`% of the runners took longer in the second half, so
doubling the split underestimated their actual finish. The model's residual
standard deviation was `r fmt(fit_summary$sigma, 2)` minutes, and the errors
were more spread out for runners with longer splits. Robust standard errors and
a log-log model supported the same pacing conclusion. The fitted equation gives
a better estimate of the average finish in this field, but individual finishing
times remain uncertain and the equation should be checked before being used for
another race.

# Introduction

If a runner reaches the halfway point of a marathon in 1 hour 45 minutes,
doubling that time gives a projected finish of 3 hours 30 minutes. The
calculation is quick, and it is easy to understand why runners and spectators
use it. However, it works exactly only when the runner completes the second
half in another 1 hour 45 minutes. Any slowdown after halfway makes the
projection too optimistic.

Running the second half more slowly than the first is called a positive split.
Previous studies have found that positive splits are common in marathons.
@march2011age and @santoslozano2014influence reported differences in pacing
across runners of different abilities. March et al. also found that slower and
less experienced runners tended to slow more. These findings suggest that the
doubling rule may work better for some runners than for others.

There are several reasons why maintaining the opening pace becomes difficult.
Runners use up stored glycogen, build up muscle damage, and may become hotter
as the race continues. Fueling, training, and conditions on the day can also
affect the second half. Earlier research found that men slowed more than women
on average [@deaner2015men], and that warmer conditions were associated with
larger pacing changes, especially among slower runners [@ely2008effect].
@smyth2021how examined more severe late-race slowdowns among recreational
runners. These studies provide useful background, but they do not give one
finishing-time equation for the field analyzed here.

In this paper, I ask two questions. First, how closely does the halfway split
predict net finishing time in the 2023 Boston Marathon? Second, does the fitted
slope differ from 2, the value expected if the two halves take equal time? A
simple linear regression is suitable for these questions because it describes
the relationship with one equation. It also gives a measure of the variation
left around the fitted line.

The benchmark matters. Regression software usually tests whether a slope is
zero. Here, that is not the main question: the halfway time is already part of
the finishing time, and a strong positive association is expected. Testing
against 2 is more useful because it compares the fitted relationship with the
doubling rule. 

The estimated slope is `r fmt(b1, 3)`. Therefore, an extra minute at halfway is
associated with about `r fmt(b1, 2)` extra minutes at the finish, including
about `r fmt(b1 - 1, 2)` extra minutes in the second half. The model explains a
large share of the variation in finishing time, but that does not make each
individual prediction precise. The conventional prediction intervals extend
about `r fmt(2 * fit_summary$sigma, 0)` minutes on either side of the fitted
value, and their accuracy varies across the field. The sections below describe
the data, explain the model and its checks, and then discuss the results and
their limits.

# Data {#sec-data}

## Source and observational units

I used the official results of the Boston Marathon held on April 17, 2023.
@fay2023boston compiled the file from results published by the
@baa2023results and made it available through the SCORE Network Sports Data
Repository. Each row represents one finisher. The full file has
`r fmt(n_finishers, 0)` finishers, so it covers the finishing field rather than
a random sample of it. Runners who started but did not finish are not
included.

The race times come from electronic timing chips. Mats along the course record
when a runner passes, and the organizer publishes the results after the race.
 It
does not show what happened between checkpoints. For example, two runners can
have identical halfway and finishing times even if one stopped briefly and the
other slowed gradually.

Since the complete finishing field is observed, the fitted line describes the
runners in this race directly. The confidence intervals and tests require a
broader interpretation. I use them as model-based measures of uncertainty for
similar runners racing under conditions like these, rather than as uncertainty
from sampling the 2023 finishing field. The data come from only one event, so
they cannot establish how stable the relationship is across races or years.

Boston also has a selective entry process. Most entrants meet a qualifying-time
standard at an earlier marathon, while other runners enter through charity
programs. Its runners are therefore not a random sample of everyone who runs
marathons. This affects how widely the results can be applied.

## Variables

The source file contains 15 columns with runner information, finishing places,
and race times. I used five columns and calculated two additional variables.
The model itself uses only net finishing time and the half-marathon split. Sex
and age group describe the field; gun time helps explain the choice of
response.

**Net finishing time** is the elapsed time between crossing the starting mat
and crossing the finishing mat. I converted it from seconds to minutes. This is
different from gun time, which begins at the official start signal. Boston uses
waves and starting corrals, so a runner may cross the starting mat several
minutes after the signal. In this file, gun time exceeds net time by a median
of `r fmt(median(all_finishers$gun_min - all_finishers$finish_min), 1)` minutes
and by as much as
`r fmt(max(all_finishers$gun_min - all_finishers$finish_min), 1)` minutes. Net
time is the appropriate response for studying the runner's pace because it
excludes this waiting time.

**Half-marathon split** is the net elapsed time at the halfway mat, also
converted to minutes. This is the explanatory variable. From the split and finishing time, I calculated the second-half time (net
finishing time minus the split) and the split ratio (second-half time divided
by the split).
A split ratio above 1 means a slower second half. A ratio below 1 means a
faster second half, and a ratio of 1 means that both halves took the same time.

Sex is recorded as M or W in the source file. Women make up
`r fmt(100 * mean(run$sex == "Women"), 1)`% of the analysis data. Age is given
in ten groups, from 18--39 to 80+, rather than as an exact value. The largest
group is 18--39, with `r fmt(100 * mean(run$age_group == "18-39"), 1)`% of
finishers; the remaining `r fmt(100 * mean(run$age_group != "18-39"), 1)`% are
aged 40 or over. Using age group as a continuous predictor would require
choosing a numerical value for each band. I did not do that here.

The times are recorded to about one second, a small amount compared with the
`r fmt(sd(run$half_min), 1)`-minute standard deviation of halfway splits. I
therefore treated timing precision as negligible for this analysis. A more
important issue is that finishing time includes the halfway split. The two
variables share part of the same measurement, so their strong association needs
to be interpreted with that structure in mind.

## Missing data and field characteristics {#sec-field}

There are `r n_dropped` finishers without a recorded half-marathon split, or
`r fmt(100 * n_dropped / n_finishers, 2)`% of the full field. A missed chip
reading is one possible explanation, although the results file does not
establish why a split is missing. Since these runners lack the predictor needed
for the model, I excluded them. This leaves `r fmt(n_analysis, 0)` runners. No
other variable used in the analysis has missing values, and there are no
duplicate runners.

The excluded runners have a mean finishing time of
`r fmt(mean(all_finishers$finish_min[is.na(all_finishers$half_min)]), 1)`
minutes, compared with `r fmt(mean(run$finish_min), 1)` minutes for those
retained. Their sex and age-group distributions are also similar to the rest of
the field. These comparisons suggest that the exclusions are unlikely to have a
large effect, but they do not prove that missing splits are unrelated to
pacing.

@tbl-summary summarizes the analysis variables. Halfway times range from
`r hms(min(run$half_min))` to `r hms(max(run$half_min))`, and net finishing
times range from `r hms(min(run$finish_min))` to `r hms(max(run$finish_min))`.
The means are above the medians for all three time variables, reflecting the
long upper tails. The median split ratio is `r fmt(median_ratio, 3)`: a runner
at the median of this ratio took about `r fmt(100 * (median_ratio - 1), 1)`%
longer for the second half.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary statistics for the 26,526 finishers with a recorded halfway split. Times are in minutes. The split ratio has no units."
describe_variable <- function(values, label, digits) {
  quartiles <- quantile(values, c(0.25, 0.75))
  data.frame(
    Variable = label,
    Mean = mean(values),
    SD = stats::sd(values),
    Min = min(values),
    Q1 = quartiles[[1]],
    Median = median(values),
    Q3 = quartiles[[2]],
    Max = max(values)
  ) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ formatC(.x, format = "f", digits = digits)))
}

summary_table <- bind_rows(
  describe_variable(run$half_min, "Half-marathon split", 1),
  describe_variable(run$finish_min, "Net finishing time", 1),
  describe_variable(run$second_half_min, "Second-half time", 1),
  describe_variable(run$split_ratio, "Split ratio", 3)
)

kable(
  summary_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", rep("r", 7))
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

The `r fmt(sum(run$sex == "Women"), 0)` women had a median finish of
`r hms(median(run$finish_min[run$sex == "Women"]))`, while the
`r fmt(sum(run$sex == "Men"), 0)` men had a median finish of
`r hms(median(run$finish_min[run$sex == "Men"]))`. Their pacing summaries were
much closer. Both groups had a median split ratio of
`r fmt(median(run$split_ratio[run$sex == "Women"]), 3)`. A slower second half
was recorded for
`r fmt(100 * mean(run$second_half_min[run$sex == "Women"] > run$half_min[run$sex == "Women"]), 1)`%
of women and
`r fmt(100 * mean(run$second_half_min[run$sex == "Men"] > run$half_min[run$sex == "Men"]), 1)`%
of men. These summaries show similar overall pacing in the two groups, although
they do not rule out differences after accounting for halfway time or age.

Comparisons with other marathons are also limited because all runners faced
the same course and race day. Earlier work links temperature
to pacing, particularly for slower runners [@ely2008effect], but this file does
not provide variation across race days that would allow me to estimate a
separate weather effect.

@fig-distributions shows the distributions of halfway time, finishing time,
and the split ratio. Both time distributions have long right tails. Most split
ratios are just above 1, consistent with a modest slowdown, but a smaller
number are much larger. Overall, `r fmt(pct_positive, 1)`% of finishers ran a
positive split.

```{r}
#| label: fig-distributions
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of halfway split, net finishing time, and split ratio. The dashed line in the right panel marks equal times for the two halves. Its horizontal axis is limited to 0.8--1.6; 0.15% of runners fall outside that range. The largest split ratio is 2.524."
p1 <- ggplot(run, aes(half_min)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "grey35", colour = NA) +
  labs(x = "Half-marathon split (min)", y = "Runners")

p2 <- ggplot(run, aes(finish_min)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "grey35", colour = NA) +
  labs(x = "Net finishing time (min)", y = "Runners")

p3 <- ggplot(run, aes(split_ratio)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, fill = "grey35", colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.8, 1.6)) +
  labs(x = "Split ratio (2nd half / 1st half)", y = "Runners")

p1 + p2 + p3
```

@fig-relationship plots finishing time against halfway time. Each point
represents a runner. The dashed line is $y = 2x$, the doubling rule. Points
above it are positive splits. The main group of points follows a roughly
straight pattern and sits mostly above the reference line. The gap also becomes
larger toward the longer halfway times. This is the pattern the regression
measures.

## Additional and alternative data

Several additional data sources could help explain the pacing pattern. The
Boston Athletic Association publishes 5 km splits, which could show where a
runner began to slow. Results from other years and other marathons would allow
comparisons across courses and conditions. Hourly weather records from the
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration could be matched to the period
when runners were on the course. Qualifying times would provide information
about recent performance before race day.

In particular, qualifying times could help distinguish a runner
whose halfway pace was unusually fast for their ability from one whose second
half was simply slower than usual. The present file cannot make that
distinction.

```{r}
#| label: fig-relationship
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-cap: "Net finishing time against halfway split before fitting the regression. Transparent points make areas with many runners appear darker. The dashed line represents equal times for the two halves, $y = 2x$."
ggplot(run, aes(half_min, finish_min)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.35, colour = "grey25") +
  geom_abline(slope = 2, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
              colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Half-marathon split (minutes)", y = "Net finishing time (minutes)")
```

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## The model

For runner $i$, let $Y_i$ be net finishing time and $x_i$ be the half-marathon
split, both in minutes. There are $n = `r fmt(n_analysis, 0)`$ runners. The
initial simple linear regression model is
$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
  \varepsilon_i \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2).$$

The intercept, $\beta_0$, is the model's expected finishing time at a halfway
split of zero. That split is impossible in a race, so the intercept is useful
for positioning the line rather than for describing an actual runner. The
slope, $\beta_1$, is the expected difference in finishing time associated with
a one-minute difference in halfway time. The error, $\varepsilon_i$, is the
difference between runner $i$'s finishing time and the conditional mean
specified by the model.

I estimated the coefficients using ordinary least squares. It chooses the line
that minimizes
$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2.$$
These are squared vertical distances from the observed points to the line.
Once the model is fitted, each residual is the runner's observed finishing time
minus their fitted finishing time. The residual standard deviation,
$\hat\sigma$, summarizes the scale of these errors in minutes.

For a halfway split of $x_0$, the predicted finishing time is
$$\hat{Y}_0 = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_0.$$
There are two different uncertainties to consider. A confidence interval for
the mean finish concerns the average finishing time of runners with that
split. A prediction interval concerns one runner's finishing time. The latter
must allow for individual differences around the line as well as uncertainty
in the estimated line, so it is much wider. A large number of observations can
make the mean estimate precise while leaving individual predictions quite
uncertain.

I used one predictor to keep the question focused on what can be estimated
from a halfway time alone. A model with age, sex, weather, and previous
performance could be useful, but it would require more information than the
halfway clock provides. 

## The even-pacing benchmark

If both halves took the same time for every runner, finishing time would
satisfy $Y_i = 2x_i$. This corresponds to $\beta_0 = 0$ and $\beta_1 = 2$. I
tested the slope against that benchmark using
$$H_0: \beta_1 = 2 \qquad \text{versus} \qquad H_1: \beta_1 \neq 2.$$
The conventional test statistic is
$$t = \frac{\hat\beta_1 - 2}{SE(\hat\beta_1)},$$
with $n - 2 = `r fmt(n_analysis - 2, 0)`$ degrees of freedom under the initial
model assumptions. This tests the slope component of the equal-pacing
relationship. A slope of 2 alone would not establish equal pacing because a
nonzero intercept could still produce a systematic difference between the
halves.

A slope above 2 means that a one-minute increase in halfway time is associated
with more than two extra minutes in total finishing time. Since one of those
minutes is already in the first half, more than one extra minute is associated
with the second half. 

A high $R^2$ needs care here, because the response contains the predictor as
one of its parts. That shared component contributes to the
strong relationship between the times; it is not independent evidence that the
model explains the causes of pacing. The estimated slope's distance from 2 and
the spread of the residuals are more useful for the questions asked here. 

## Assumptions and diagnostics {#sec-assumptions}

I examined the main regression assumptions with plots and diagnostic summaries.

**Linearity.** The model assumes that mean finishing time changes at a constant
rate as halfway time increases. I checked the scatterplot and a plot of
residuals against fitted values for curvature. The main pattern is
approximately straight, and the residual plot does not show a strong curved
trend. A straight line is therefore a reasonable summary of the average
relationship over the observed range.

**Independence.** The model treats the errors of different runners as
unrelated. This is difficult to justify fully in a race. Runners may follow the
same pacing group, run together, or respond similarly to course conditions.
Dependence of this kind can make usual standard errors too small. It does not
automatically bias the fitted coefficients if the conditional mean model is
correct, but the results file cannot verify that condition or identify all such
groups. The HC1 check below addresses unequal variance, not dependence between
runners.

**Constant variance.** The initial model assumes the same error variance at
every halfway time. The residual plot shows that this assumption does not hold
well: the band becomes wider as fitted times increase. The residual standard
deviation is `r fmt(min(spread_raw$resid_sd), 1)` minutes in the fastest tenth
of the halfway-split distribution and `r fmt(max(spread_raw$resid_sd), 1)`
minutes in the slowest tenth. That is about a `r fmt(spread_ratio_raw, 1)`-fold
increase. The Breusch--Pagan test also rejects constant variance, with
$BP = `r fmt(diag$bp_test$statistic, 1)`$ on `r diag$bp_test$parameter` degree
of freedom and $p < 0.001$ [@breusch1979simple; @zeileis2002lmtest].

**Normality.** The model assumes normally distributed errors. A histogram of
the residuals is centered near zero, but it is not symmetric: it is right
skewed, with a long upper tail of runners who finished much later than
predicted, and both tails are heavier than a normal curve would give. With a
large data set, slope inference can be less
sensitive to nonnormal errors under suitable regularity and dependence
conditions. This does not make the individual errors normal. Prediction
intervals based on a normal error distribution remain approximations.

I also examined Cook's distance to assess how strongly individual observations
affect the fitted line. The largest value is `r fmt(diag$max_cooks, 3)`, below
the commonly used reference value of 1.  I retained unusual pacing results rather than
excluding them just because they were far from the main group. Large residuals
may represent real race outcomes, and the file alone does not show that they
are recording errors.

@fig-diagnostics brings these checks together. Its main concern is the
increasing spread of the errors, rather than obvious curvature. The bottom
panel compares that spread on the original and log-log scales. Logging the
times reduces the increase across the field, but it does not eliminate it.

## Model selection and validation {#sec-selection}

I considered a model in minutes and a model using the natural logarithms of
both times. I chose the original scale for the main analysis because its
coefficients are easier to connect to the doubling rule. The slope can be
compared directly with 2, and the residual standard deviation is expressed in
minutes. I used the log-log fit to check whether the pacing conclusion depended
on this choice of scale. The two models have different response variables, so
comparing their $R^2$ values directly would not be a suitable way to choose
between them.

Unequal variance affects the uncertainty calculations for the original model.
If the conditional mean is correctly specified, ordinary least squares can
still estimate the mean relationship without bias. However, the conventional
standard errors assume a common variance and may be misleading here. A
prediction interval using one residual standard deviation also cannot
represent both the narrow spread among faster runners and the wider spread
among slower ones.

I first recalculated the slope's standard error with a
heteroskedasticity-consistent HC1 estimator [@zeileis2004sandwich]. This allows
observations to contribute different amounts of error variance to the
uncertainty estimate. It changes the standard error and confidence interval
without changing the fitted line. As noted above, it does not account for
runners' errors being correlated.

The second check was the log-log model,
$$\log(Y_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 \log(x_i) + \eta_i.$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.1
#| fig-cap: "Regression diagnostics. The residual plot shows increasing spread at longer fitted times. The histogram of residuals is centered near zero but is right skewed, with a long upper tail; its horizontal axis is limited to $-60$ to 90 minutes. The bottom panel gives residual standard deviations within tenths of the halfway-split distribution, relative to the fastest tenth. Spread increases about 2.4-fold on the original scale and 1.4-fold on the log-log scale."
aug <- diag$augmented

d1 <- ggplot(aug, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.3, colour = "grey25") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Fitted finishing time (min)", y = "Residual (min)",
       title = "Residuals vs fitted")

d2 <- ggplot(aug, aes(resid)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "grey35", colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-60, 90)) +
  labs(x = "Residual (min)", y = "Runners",
       title = "Histogram of residuals")

spread_compare <- bind_rows(
  spread_raw %>%
    transmute(split = mean_predictor,
              relative_sd = resid_sd / resid_sd[1],
              Model = "Original scale"),
  spread_log %>%
    transmute(split = exp(mean_predictor),
              relative_sd = resid_sd / resid_sd[1],
              Model = "Log-log scale")
)

d3 <- ggplot(spread_compare, aes(split, relative_sd, colour = Model, shape = Model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Original scale" = "#2166AC", "Log-log scale" = "#B2182B")) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean half-marathon split within decile (minutes)",
    y = "Residual SD relative\nto fastest decile",
    title = "Growth in residual spread across the field",
    colour = NULL, shape = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

(d1 + d2) / d3
```

Here, $\gamma_1$ is an elasticity. A 1% increase in halfway time is associated
with approximately a $\gamma_1$% increase in finishing time. Under equal
pacing,
$$\log(Y_i) = \log(2) + \log(x_i),$$
so the slope benchmark is 1 and the intercept benchmark is $\log(2)$. Logging
the variables compresses their long upper tails and can reduce the change in
error spread. In this analysis it improves variance stability, although some
unequal spread remains. Agreement between the two checks supports the main
slope conclusion; it does not establish that all regression assumptions have
been satisfied.



## Possible extensions to the model

Adding sex and age group, together with interactions with the halfway split,
would allow separate slopes for different groups. The similar overall split
ratios for men and women do not tell us what those adjusted slopes would be.
 Such a model would also need more information
from a runner than the single split used here.

A quadratic term or a spline could allow the average relationship to bend. The
diagnostic plot does not show strong curvature, so I did not make this the
primary model. 

Weighted least squares could account for different amounts of error variance
across halfway times, provided that suitable weights were estimated. Quantile
regression could estimate selected finishing-time percentiles rather than only
the mean. This would be useful for constructing prediction limits that vary
with the split. 

## Software

The analysis was carried out in R version
`r paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".")` [@rcore2024]. I used
`dplyr` for data handling [@wickham2023dplyr] and `readr` to read the data
[@wickham2024readr]. Figures were made with `ggplot2` [@wickham2016ggplot2] and
combined using `patchwork` [@pedersen2024patchwork]. Robust standard errors came
from `sandwich` [@zeileis2004sandwich; @zeileis2020sandwich], and regression
diagnostic tests used `lmtest` [@zeileis2002lmtest]. The report used Quarto
[@allaire2022quarto], `knitr` [@xie2023knitr], and `kableExtra`
[@zhu2024kableextra]. The regressions were fitted with `lm` in R's `stats`
package.

# Results {#sec-results}

## The fitted model

The fitted line, with coefficients rounded for display, is
$$\widehat{\text{finish}} = `r fmt(b0, 2)` + `r fmt(b1, 3)` \times
  \text{half-marathon split}.$$
Both times are in minutes. @tbl-coefs gives the coefficient estimates,
conventional standard errors, and confidence intervals.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coefs
#| tbl-cap: "Ordinary least squares estimates for net finishing time regressed on halfway split. The confidence intervals are conventional 95% intervals. The HC1 interval for the slope is 2.210--2.225."
coef_table <- data.frame(
  Term = c("Intercept", "Half-marathon split"),
  Estimate = c(b0, b1),
  `Standard error` = c(fit_summary$coefficients[1, 2], fit_summary$coefficients[2, 2]),
  `CI low` = confint(primary)[, 1],
  `CI high` = confint(primary)[, 2],
  check.names = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(Estimate, `CI low`, `CI high`),
           ~ formatC(.x, format = "f", digits = 3)),
    `Standard error` = formatC(`Standard error`, format = "g", digits = 3)
  )

kable(
  coef_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

The slope is above the equal-pacing benchmark of 2. Comparing it with that
value gives $t = `r fmt(slope_classical$t_statistic, 1)`$ on
`r fmt(slope_classical$df, 0)` degrees of freedom, with $p < 0.001$. The
conventional 95% confidence interval, `r fmt(slope_classical$conf_low, 3)`--`r fmt(slope_classical$conf_high, 3)`,
is entirely above 2. For runners whose halfway times differ by one minute, the
model estimates a difference of about `r fmt(b1, 2)` minutes at the finish. Of
that difference, one minute is in the first half and about `r fmt(b1 - 1, 2)`
minutes is in the second half.

The negative intercept should not be interpreted as an actual finishing time. A
zero-minute halfway split is impossible and is far outside the observed range
of `r fmt(min(run$half_min), 1)`--`r fmt(max(run$half_min), 1)` minutes. The
intercept helps place the fitted line through the data. 

The model has $R^2 = `r fmt(fit_summary$r.squared, 3)`$, and the correlation
between halfway and finishing times is
`r fmt(cor(run$half_min, run$finish_min), 3)`. These values show a close
relationship in the observed field, but part of that relationship comes from
finishing time containing halfway time. The residual standard deviation is
`r fmt(fit_summary$sigma, 2)` minutes. This describes the scale of errors
around the line; it is not a guarantee that a runner will finish within
`r fmt(fit_summary$sigma, 2)` minutes of the prediction, nor is it the mean
absolute prediction error.

@fig-scatter adds the fitted line to the scatterplot. It crosses the doubling
line at a halfway time of about `r hms(split_crossing)`. Only
`r n_below_crossing` runners reached halfway sooner than that. For all of the
remaining field, the model predicts a finish later than simple doubling would
predict. The difference grows with halfway time. This model comparison should
be distinguished from the observed `r fmt(pct_positive, 1)`% positive-split
rate: a runner can still finish above or below either prediction.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: 'The fitted regression line and the doubling rule. The solid line is $\widehat{\text{finish}} = -14.53 + 2.218 \times \text{split}$; the dashed line is $\text{finish} = 2 \times \text{split}$. They cross near a 1:07 halfway time. Above that split, the fitted projection is later than the doubling projection.'
ggplot(run, aes(half_min, finish_min)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.35, colour = "grey25") +
  geom_abline(
    aes(slope = 2, intercept = 0, linetype = "Even pacing (y = 2x)"),
    colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    aes(slope = b1, intercept = b0, linetype = "Fitted regression"),
    colour = "#2166AC", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Even pacing (y = 2x)" = "dashed", "Fitted regression" = "solid"),
    name = NULL,
    guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(
      colour = c("#B2182B", "#2166AC"), linewidth = 0.7
    ))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Half-marathon split (minutes)", y = "Net finishing time (minutes)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## What the model means for a runner

@tbl-predictions gives projected finishing times for five halfway splits. It
compares the doubling rule with the fitted model and includes approximate 95%
prediction intervals for individual runners. The last column is the difference
between the model projection and the doubling projection, rather than the
actual prediction error for a particular runner.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictions
#| tbl-cap: "Finishing-time projections from five halfway splits. Prediction intervals use the original model's common residual standard deviation and are approximate because error spread changes across the field and the residuals have heavy tails."
pred_points <- data.frame(half_min = c(90, 105, 120, 135, 150))
pred_fit <- predict(primary, newdata = pred_points, interval = "prediction")

pred_table <- data.frame(
  Halfway = vapply(pred_points$half_min, hms, character(1)),
  Doubling = vapply(2 * pred_points$half_min, hms, character(1)),
  Model = vapply(pred_fit[, "fit"], hms, character(1)),
  `95% prediction interval` = paste0(
    vapply(pred_fit[, "lwr"], hms, character(1)), " to ",
    vapply(pred_fit[, "upr"], hms, character(1))
  ),
  Difference = paste0(
    formatC(pred_fit[, "fit"] - 2 * pred_points$half_min, format = "f", digits = 1),
    " min"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(
  pred_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "r")
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

At a 1:30 halfway time, the model adds about `r fmt(shortfall(90), 0)` minutes
to the doubled split. At 2:00, it adds nearly `r fmt(shortfall(120), 0)`
minutes. At 2:30, it adds about `r fmt(shortfall(150), 0)` minutes. For the
median halfway split of `r hms(median_split)`, the difference is about
`r fmt(shortfall_median, 0)` minutes. Differences of around a quarter of an
hour or more occur near the slowest tenth of the field by halfway time. The
doubling rule is therefore much closer to the fitted mean for faster runners
than for slower runners.

One rough mental calculation is to double the halfway split and add about one
minute for every five minutes beyond a split of 1:07. This approximates the
fitted correction, since
$$\widehat{\text{finish}} - 2x = `r fmt(b0, 2)` + `r fmt(b1 - 2, 3)`x.$$
The rule of thumb uses an increase of 0.2 rather than `r fmt(b1 - 2, 3)`
minutes per minute, so it is only an approximation. 

The prediction intervals in the table are about
`r fmt(diff(pred_fit[1, c("lwr", "upr")]), 0)` minutes wide. For example, the
model projection for a 1:45 split is `r hms(pred_fit[2, "fit"])`, but the
conventional interval extends from `r hms(pred_fit[2, "lwr"])` to
`r hms(pred_fit[2, "upr"])`. The large field makes the mean relationship
precise; it does not remove the variation in what individual runners do after
halfway. Training, fueling, fatigue, and conditions can all affect that part of
the race, and they are not separately measured here.

## Robustness of the pacing conclusion

@tbl-sensitivity compares the main model with the two checks. HC1 increases the
slope standard error from about `r fmt(slope_classical$std_error, 4)` to
`r fmt(slope_robust$std_error, 4)`, roughly a
`r fmt(slope_robust$std_error / slope_classical$std_error, 1)`-fold increase.
The resulting interval is
`r fmt(slope_robust$conf_low, 3)`--`r fmt(slope_robust$conf_high, 3)`, and the
test against 2 gives $t = `r fmt(slope_robust$t_statistic, 1)`$. Thus, allowing
unequal error variance still leaves the estimated slope well above the
equal-pacing benchmark.

The log-log slope is `r fmt(coef(log_model)[[2]], 3)`, compared with its
benchmark of 1, with $t = `r fmt(log_slope$t_statistic, 1)`$. On that scale, a
1% longer halfway time is associated with approximately a
`r fmt(coef(log_model)[[2]], 3)`% longer total finishing time. The direction of
the pacing result agrees with the original model. The change in residual spread
across tenths is also smaller: about `r fmt(spread_ratio_log, 1)`-fold on the
log-log scale instead of `r fmt(spread_ratio_raw, 1)`-fold on the original
scale. However, this is a reduction in unequal spread, not its complete
removal.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Checks of the slope conclusion. The benchmark is 2 on the original scale and 1 on the log-log scale. Slopes and standard errors are rounded for display; the $t$ statistics were computed from unrounded values."
sens_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c(
    "Original scale, conventional SE",
    "Original scale, robust HC1 SE",
    "Log-log scale, conventional SE"
  ),
  Slope = formatC(c(b1, b1, coef(log_model)[[2]]), format = "f", digits = 3),
  `Standard error` = formatC(
    c(slope_classical$std_error, slope_robust$std_error, log_slope$std_error),
    format = "f", digits = 4
  ),
  Benchmark = c("2", "2", "1"),
  t = formatC(
    c(slope_classical$t_statistic, slope_robust$t_statistic, log_slope$t_statistic),
    format = "f", digits = 1
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(
  sens_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r")
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

These checks support the slope result, but they do not correct the
original-scale prediction intervals in @tbl-predictions. Those intervals have
nearly the same width at every split because they use one residual standard
deviation. The observed spread is smaller among faster runners and larger among
slower runners, so a single width is likely to be too wide at the faster end
and too narrow at the slower end.

For a rough comparison, multiplying the fastest tenth's residual standard
deviation of `r fmt(min(spread_raw$resid_sd), 1)` minutes by 1.96 gives about
`r fmt(1.96 * min(spread_raw$resid_sd), 0)` minutes. Doing the same with the
slowest tenth's `r fmt(max(spread_raw$resid_sd), 1)` minutes gives about
`r fmt(1.96 * max(spread_raw$resid_sd), 0)` minutes. Both differ considerably
from the common margin of about
`r fmt(diff(pred_fit[1, c("lwr", "upr")]) / 2, 1)` minutes used in the table.
These calculations illustrate the change in spread; they are not separately
validated 95% prediction intervals, particularly given the heavy tails.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

For the 2023 Boston Marathon finishers analyzed here, the halfway split and
finishing time have a strong, approximately linear relationship. The fitted
slope is `r fmt(b1, 3)`, above the value of 2 associated with equal halves.
About `r fmt(pct_positive, 0)`% of runners actually ran a slower second half.
Taken together, these results show why doubling the halfway time is usually
optimistic for this field.

The size of the model correction matters more for slower runners. It is about
`r fmt(shortfall(90), 0)` minutes at a 1:30 split, about
`r fmt(shortfall_median, 0)` minutes at the median split, and about
`r fmt(shortfall(150), 0)` minutes at a 2:30 split.  Its pattern agrees with
earlier findings that pacing varies with runner ability
[@march2011age; @santoslozano2014influence]. The present analysis provides an
equation for this race's complete observed finishing field rather than only
comparisons between broad ability groups.

However, a precise slope does not make a precise prediction for every runner.
The overall residual standard deviation is `r fmt(fit_summary$sigma, 2)`
minutes, and the conventional individual prediction intervals extend roughly
`r fmt(2 * fit_summary$sigma, 0)` minutes on either side of the fitted value.
Their width also hides the change in error spread across halfway times. A
projected finish should be treated as an estimate of the mean at that split,
with substantial individual variation still possible.

The missing nonfinishers are an important limitation. Their absence means that
this analysis describes only runners who completed the race. Some nonfinishers
may have experienced severe fatigue or other problems, but their outcomes cannot
be inferred from the finishing file. In particular, the results do not
establish an average finishing-time slowdown for all starters or a numerical
lower bound on it. The selective Boston field also limits generalization. A
different course, field, or race day could produce a different slope and a
different amount of prediction error.

The assumptions create further limits. Error variance increases across the
field, and the residuals have heavy tails. HC1 standard errors leave the main
slope conclusion unchanged, but they do not repair the individual prediction
intervals.  Neither check
accounts for dependence among runners who race together. With only one event, I
cannot separate weather and course conditions from the relationship measured
on that day.

This is an observational, descriptive model. It does not show that making the
first half faster will cause a runner to finish sooner. Faster runners may have
better fitness, more training, or a different racing history. A runner changing
their own opening pace is not the same as comparing two runners with different
halfway times. 

Several follow-up analyses would be useful. Sex and age-group interactions
could test whether the split-to-finish relationship differs across groups, as
the earlier pacing literature suggests [@deaner2015men]. Multiple years and
weather measurements could assess stability across race days and investigate
temperature effects [@ely2008effect]. The organizers' 5 km splits would help
locate the onset of a slowdown instead of combining all second-half behavior
into one time, which would be relevant to the late-race collapse studied by
@smyth2021how.

For practical prediction, a model of the finishing-time distribution would be
especially helpful. Quantile regression could produce limits that change with
halfway time, and validation on another race or year could show how well those
limits perform. Until those checks are made, the fitted equation is a useful
summary of the 2023 Boston finishers, with the clearest result being that the
gap between simple doubling and the fitted mean becomes larger as halfway time
increases.
